runs.text:
The light came slowly over the low hills, and the village
woke to the sound of a single bell. Doors opened, pots
were set on stoves, and the smell of bread drifted along
the narrow street that ran down to the river.
You could walk its whole length before the sun cleared
the roof of the old mill, and no one hurried.

Beyond the bridge the road turned to gravel and then to
grass. Marta counted the turns she had learned as a child:
first the bent willow, then the stone with a flat top, then
the place where the stream crossed the path. She counted
them now out of habit, and because counting kept her even.

Home was a house with a blue door and a garden that never
quite kept to its beds. Mint grew through the bricks and
tomatoes leaned on the fence, and in August the whole yard
smelled of warm leaves and dust.

Her grandmother had planted the pear tree in the first
year they lived there. It was still small enough to shade
only the corner of the wall, but in autumn it gave four or
five fruits, enough for the whole street to taste.

The evening ended the way it always did, with chairs
carried out to the pavement and the neighbours arguing
gently about weather and prices, until the first lamps
came on and the children were called in.
